description: Tasks to help prepare when a parent's death is expected

tasks.title: Have a conversation about their wishes
tasks.description: Talk with your parent about their end-of-life wishes: burial vs. cremation, funeral preferences, who they want notified, and any specific requests. This conversation is hard but invaluable.
tasks.why_it_matters: Knowing their wishes reduces stress and decision-making burden later. It also honors them by ensuring things are done the way they wanted.
tips: Start gently: 'I want to make sure we honor what you want'
It's okay to have this conversation in pieces over time
Write down or record their wishes so you remember details
Ask about music, readings, or people they'd want involved in a service
Some people find it easier to discuss through a questionnaire or workbook

tasks.title: Find out if they have a will
tasks.description: Ask your parent if they have a will and where it's located. If they don't have one, gently discuss whether they'd like to create one while they're still able.
tasks.why_it_matters: A will prevents family disputes, ensures assets go where intended, and names an executor. Without one, state law decides everything—which may not match their wishes.
tips: Ask if they've worked with an attorney or used an online service
The will should name an executor—ask if that's you or someone else
If they're resistant, a simple 'I just want to be prepared' can help
Simple wills can be done online (LegalZoom, Trust & Will) for a few hundred dollars
Some hospice social workers can help facilitate these conversations

tasks.title: Understand their financial picture
tasks.description: Learn what accounts, assets, and debts your parent has. You don't need every detail—just a general map of where things are.
tasks.why_it_matters: After someone dies, you need to find and notify all financial institutions. Knowing what exists makes this much easier.
tips: Ask: 'Which banks do you use?' 'Do you have any investment accounts?'
Check if they have a list of accounts somewhere
Ask about debts: mortgage, car loans, credit cards
Don't forget retirement accounts (401k, IRA, pension)
Ask about life insurance policies—many people forget they have them

tasks.title: Check beneficiary designations
tasks.description: Help your parent review beneficiaries on life insurance, retirement accounts, and bank accounts. These designations override the will.
tasks.why_it_matters: Beneficiary designations pass assets directly—they trump the will. Outdated beneficiaries (like an ex-spouse) can cause major problems.
tips: Check life insurance policies, 401(k), IRA, and bank accounts
Ask if beneficiaries were updated after any divorces or deaths
POD (payable on death) and TOD (transfer on death) designations on accounts
Consider if percentages still make sense given current circumstances

tasks.title: Find out where important documents are
tasks.description: Ask your parent where they keep important papers: will, insurance policies, deeds, Social Security card, birth certificate, marriage certificate.
tasks.why_it_matters: Searching for documents while grieving is exhausting. Knowing where things are now saves enormous stress later.
tips: Ask about safe deposit boxes—where's the key and which bank?
Check for a fireproof safe at their home
Ask if they have a filing system or if papers are scattered
Get contact info for their attorney, accountant, financial advisor
Consider taking photos of document locations so you remember

tasks.title: Discuss power of attorney
tasks.description: Ask if your parent has designated someone with power of attorney for finances and healthcare. If not, discuss setting this up while they're still mentally competent.
tasks.why_it_matters: Power of attorney allows you to manage finances and make healthcare decisions if they become unable to. Without it, you may need expensive court proceedings.
tips: There are two types: financial POA and healthcare POA (or healthcare proxy)
The person must be mentally competent to sign these documents
POA ends at death—it doesn't give authority over the estate
Consider a 'springing' POA that only activates if they become incapacitated
Many elder law attorneys can set these up quickly

tasks.title: Understand their healthcare wishes
tasks.description: Discuss and document your parent's wishes for end-of-life medical care: DNR status, life support preferences, organ donation, and comfort care priorities.
tasks.why_it_matters: Clear advance directives prevent family conflicts and ensure your parent's wishes are followed, even if they can't communicate.
tips: Ask about DNR (Do Not Resuscitate) preferences
Discuss comfort care vs. aggressive treatment
Ask about organ and tissue donation wishes
Make sure their doctor has a copy of any advance directive
Hospice can help facilitate these conversations if you're working with them

tasks.title: Learn about digital accounts and passwords
tasks.description: Find out what email, social media, and online accounts your parent has. Discuss how you might access these later if needed.
tasks.why_it_matters: After death, you may need to access email to find account information, notify contacts, or close accounts. This is nearly impossible without passwords.
tips: Ask if they use a password manager
Email is the most important—it's used to recover other accounts
Ask about auto-pay bills that might need to be cancelled
Discuss their wishes for social media (memorialize, delete, etc.)
Some services offer legacy contacts (Apple, Facebook, Google)

tasks.title: Consider pre-planning funeral arrangements
tasks.description: If your parent is interested, help them pre-plan (and potentially pre-pay) funeral arrangements. This removes decisions and costs from grieving family members.
tasks.why_it_matters: Pre-planning removes burden from family, locks in current prices, and ensures their specific wishes are documented.
tips: Pre-paying isn't required—pre-planning the details alone is valuable
If pre-paying, ensure the money is protected (trust or insurance)
Get everything in writing
Share the pre-plan location with family members
Review periodically—circumstances and wishes can change

tasks.title: Connect with other family members
tasks.description: Touch base with siblings or other family members about your parent's situation. Discuss who will handle what, and try to get on the same page before crisis hits.
tasks.why_it_matters: Family conflicts often erupt during end-of-life and after death. Discussing expectations now prevents misunderstandings and hurt feelings later.
tips: Discuss who will be the main point of contact for medical staff
Talk about caregiving responsibilities if applicable
Address any existing family tensions before they're amplified by grief
Be clear about executor role and responsibilities
Consider a family meeting (in person or video) to align on plans

tasks.title: Take care of yourself during this time
tasks.description: Anticipatory grief is real and exhausting. Make sure you're taking care of your own physical and emotional needs during this difficult time.
tasks.why_it_matters: You can't pour from an empty cup. Taking care of yourself isn't selfish—it's necessary to be present for your parent and handle what's ahead.
tips: Anticipatory grief can be as intense as grief after death
It's okay to feel relief alongside sadness—that's normal
Consider talking to a therapist or grief counselor now
Lean on friends and family for support
Take breaks when you need them—you don't have to be present every moment
